standard.title: Reflect on own and others' music to inform choices
standard.description: use listening, aural skills and understanding of the information provided in scores, charts or lead-sheets to develop interpretations and reflect on the practices of others to inform their own
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have developed aural skills for tuning/intonation and used recordings and performance comparisons to develop interpretations (AC9AMU8D02 — Y7-8). They can read from scores and lead-sheets during performance. The Y9-10 step requires using focused listening and aural/memory skills to identify, sing/play and notate musical ideas for future use, and developing real-time intonation skills.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use listening, aural skills and score/chart/lead-sheet information to develop interpretations, and reflect on the practices of others to inform their own compositions and performances.

nodes.label: Developing interpretations from scores and listening
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use both score/chart/lead-sheet information and listening to develop a personal interpretation — identifying what the notation specifies, what it leaves open, and how listening to other performances informs their choices.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two interpretive decisions for a piece: one specified by the score/chart and one left open; explain how they decided on the open decision.
nodes.typical_width: Use scores, charts and lead-sheets alongside listening to multiple recordings to develop a documented personal interpretation; identify what the notation specifies (pitches, rhythms, dynamics markings) vs what it leaves to the performer (articulation nuance, tempo flexibility, expression); explain choices with reference to both score and listening.
wider: Analyse three recordings of the same piece — document the specific interpretive differences in each and use the analysis to develop a personal interpretation that draws on the strengths of all three
Compare how much interpretive freedom is available in different notation formats (a highly prescriptive score vs a lead-sheet vs a chord chart) — discuss how each format shapes the performer's role
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that scores specify some things and leave others to the performer is the conceptual foundation of music interpretation. Students who treat every marking as fixed cannot develop an interpretation; those who ignore notation produce performances that disregard the composer's intentions. The interplay between what is specified and what is open is where interpretation lives.

response_modes.reason: Make the specification/interpretation distinction explicit for each piece studied. Use a two-column annotation: 'What the score specifies' vs 'What I decide.' For open decisions, require at least one listening reference. This makes the interpretive process visible and accountable.

success_criteria: Can distinguish between score-specified and performer-decided aspects of an interpretation
Has a documented interpretive decision for at least two open aspects, each with a stated reason

nodes.label: Aural and memory skills for capturing musical ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use focused listening and aural/memory skills to identify, sing or play, and notate or document musical ideas (pitch patterns, intervals, chord progressions) for future use in composition or performance.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and notate or record at least one musical idea heard during listening (a melodic motif, a chord progression, or a rhythmic pattern) with sufficient accuracy to reproduce it later.
nodes.typical_width: Use focused listening to build a personal vocabulary of musical ideas — identifying characteristic pitch patterns, intervals and chord progressions in diverse styles; singing or playing back what is heard; documenting using notation or recording; using captured ideas as raw material for composition or improvisation.
wider: Transcribe a short melody or chord progression by ear, document the process, and use the transcription as the basis for a composition or arrangement
Develop a personal resource of captured musical ideas from multiple styles — organise them by type (melodic, harmonic, rhythmic) and use them deliberately in an original composition

response_modes.reason: A personal musical vocabulary built through listening is a composing resource that no technique exercise can substitute for. The habit of capturing interesting musical ideas when encountered — rather than passively hearing them — builds the compositional raw material that makes original work richer.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Building a personal library of musical ideas from diverse styles is one of the most valuable long-term habits a developing musician can form — it directly feeds compositional originality and stylistic fluency.
success_criteria: Can identify and notate or record at least one musical idea from listening with sufficient accuracy to reproduce it
Has used at least one captured idea deliberately in a subsequent composition or improvisation

nodes.label: Real-time intonation in performance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can monitor and adjust intonation in real time during ensemble performance, demonstrating developing ability to hear and correct pitch discrepancies without stopping.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate at least one real-time intonation adjustment during ensemble performance; describe what they heard and how they adjusted.
nodes.typical_width: Develop and refine real-time intonation skills across ensemble contexts — hearing pitch discrepancies while playing, adjusting immediately, using aural reference points (root of chord, unison pitch) to calibrate; compare real-time adjustment vs stopping and correcting.
wider: Work in a small ensemble specifically on intonation awareness — use slow-tempo practice, tuning drones and unison passages to develop aural sensitivity before applying it in full tempo performance
Develop a personal practice routine for intonation — identify consistent problem pitches or intervals, practise targeted exercises and track improvement through recording comparison

response_modes.reason: Real-time intonation requires aural sensitivity that is developed through sustained, focused practice — not episodic attention. The consolidation investment is in making intonation awareness a consistent rehearsal focus rather than an occasional correction, so that the aural monitoring becomes automatic rather than deliberate.

success_criteria: Demonstrates at least one real-time intonation adjustment during ensemble performance
Can describe the aural reference they used to detect and correct the intonation issue
